articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Oil Traders and Government-Linked Facilitators; Issues New Cuba FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting Iranian oil traders and government-linked facilitators. These individuals and entities are accused of assisting Tehran in selling oil abroad and misappropriating the proceeds. The action falls under Operation Economic Outcast, utilizing executive orders related to Iran's petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, as well as counterterrorism authorities.

Among those sanctioned are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former intelligence officer with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Majid Taj, identified as the brother of the head of the Iranian Football Federation.
Additionally, OFAC issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations; Issues Illicit Drugs GL and Amended Russia-related GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related activities.
In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued Illicit Drugs General License 1, which authorizes the wind down of transactions involving certain persons blocked on November 19, 2026.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License, specifically General License 131L, which authorizes certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has implemented new counter terrorism designations. These actions aim to disrupt financial networks and support structures for terrorist organizations globally.

The specific individuals and entities targeted by these designations were added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. Further details regarding the designated parties and the nature of their involvement in terrorism financing were made available on OFAC's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting several Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations for their involvement in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.

Among the entities added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List are 'LOS LORENZANAS' (also known as 'LORENZANA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION', 'THE LORENZANA CLAN', and 'THE LORENZANA FAMILY'), and 'LOS MENDOZA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION'.
These designations highlight the nexus between drug trafficking and terrorism, aiming to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of these criminal organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Update to Iran Designation Listings
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has published an update to certain Iran-related designations. This action involves modifications to existing listings on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

These updates are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the effectiveness and accuracy of its sanctions programs targeting Iran. The specific changes to the listings were detailed on OFAC's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, targeting individuals and entities involved in activities deemed to support the Iranian regime. These actions are part of the ongoing pressure campaign against Iran.

The designations aim to disrupt networks that contribute to Iran's destabilizing activities in the region and its pursuit of illicit programs. Further details on the specific parties designated were made available on OFAC's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Imposes New Cuba Sanctions and Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt illicit activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
Concurrently, OFAC imposed new designations related to Cuba, targeting a crude oil shipping network, state-owned entities, and China-based suppliers of Cuba's military forces.
Additionally, OFAC published a Cuba-related determination, extending Executive Order 14404 to four additional sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Updates Listings, Issues Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities.

OFAC also published an Iran-related Alert titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion,' highlighting the risks associated with providing services to vessels using deceptive practices to circumvent sanctions.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License, specifically General License 5AA, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or After December 18, 2026,' and an amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 595.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions related to Iran.
The specific details of the amended General License were made available on OFAC's website, providing guidance for those engaging in authorized activities involving Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities and individuals connected to North Korea. These actions aim to counter the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's (DPRK) illicit activities, including its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs.

Concurrently, OFAC also imposed designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These designations target actors involved in destabilizing activities and human rights abuses within the region.

body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement on October 27, 2026.

The specific details of the apparent violations were outlined in OFAC's enforcement release, which is publicly available. This settlement underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts across various industries to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs.
The settlement, announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 13, 2026, was part of a larger coordinated enforcement action that also involved FinCEN and the OCC.
The apparent violations involved transactions related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism, occurring between September 2021 and April 2025.

body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement on September 10, 2026.

The enforcement action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for sanctions breaches, even when they are not corporate entities. The specific nature of the violations was detailed in the public enforcement release.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of U.S. sanctions on Iran.

The violations occurred when its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), with knowledge that the goods were ultimately destined for Iran.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed by Rice Lake, which promptly launched an investigation and implemented compliance program improvements upon discovering the issue.

body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle potential civil liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement on February 25, 2026. The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021, underscoring OFAC's long-term enforcement capabilities.
This case serves as a reminder that individuals, not just corporations, are subject to U.S. sanctions laws and can face significant penalties for non-compliance.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Settles with OFAC for $1,720,000 for Kingpin Act Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations.

The violations, which occurred over a five-year period, involved entering into tuition enrollment agreements and processing 89 related financial transactions for the benefit of children of two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act.

OFAC emphasized that academic institutions, despite often perceiving themselves as low-risk, face significant sanctions exposure due to international student bodies and foreign payors, necessitating robust risk-based controls and screening procedures.

articles.headline: Global Markets React to Geopolitical Tensions and Inflation Concerns
body: Global financial markets are showing volatility as investors react to escalating geopolitical tensions and persistent inflation concerns. Major indices experienced fluctuations throughout the week, with particular attention on energy prices and their potential impact on corporate earnings.

Analysts suggest that the ongoing conflicts in Eastern Europe and the Middle East are contributing to market uncertainty, leading to a cautious approach among investors. Central bank statements regarding future interest rate hikes are also being closely watched for their implications on economic growth.

Energy prices, especially crude oil, have seen upward pressure due to supply concerns stemming from the geopolitical landscape, further fueling inflation worries and impacting various sectors of the global economy.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Signals Continued Vigilance on Inflation, Hints at Future Rate Hikes
body: The U.S. Federal Reserve, in its latest commentary, indicated a continued hawkish stance on inflation, suggesting that further interest rate hikes might be necessary to bring price stability. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell reiterated the central bank's commitment to achieving its 2% inflation target.

Market participants are now closely scrutinizing upcoming economic data, particularly consumer price index (CPI) reports and employment figures, for clues on the timing and magnitude of future rate adjustments. The Fed's cautious tone reflects the persistent challenges in taming inflationary pressures.
The prospect of higher borrowing costs continues to influence bond yields and the U.S. dollar, with implications for global capital flows and emerging markets.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Surge Amidst Middle East Tensions and Supply Disruptions
body: Global oil prices experienced a significant surge this week, driven by heightened tensions in the Middle East and concerns over potential supply disruptions. Both Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) benchmarks saw notable gains, impacting energy markets worldwide.

The escalation of geopolitical events in key oil-producing regions has fueled fears of reduced crude output, leading to increased volatility in futures markets. Traders are closely monitoring developments for any signs of further supply constraints or resolutions.
The rising cost of oil is expected to exert additional inflationary pressure on economies globally, affecting transportation, manufacturing, and consumer spending.

articles.headline: Humanitarian Crisis Deepens in Gaza Amidst Ongoing Conflict
body: The humanitarian crisis in Gaza has reportedly deepened significantly this week, with international aid organizations warning of severe shortages of food, water, and medical supplies. Ongoing conflict and restrictions on aid access are exacerbating the dire situation for civilians.

Reports from the ground indicate widespread displacement and a critical lack of essential services, leading to growing concerns about public health and the well-being of the population. Calls for a sustained ceasefire and unimpeded humanitarian access have intensified from global bodies.
Diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the conflict and facilitate aid delivery continue, but progress remains limited amidst persistent hostilities.

articles.headline: Fighting Intensifies in Eastern Ukraine as Winter Approaches
body: Fighting has reportedly intensified in eastern Ukraine as winter weather conditions begin to set in, posing new challenges for both sides of the conflict. Military analysts suggest that both Ukrainian and Russian forces are attempting to gain strategic advantages before the full onset of winter.

Reports indicate increased shelling and ground engagements in key areas, leading to further civilian casualties and infrastructure damage. International observers continue to monitor the situation closely, expressing concerns about the humanitarian impact of prolonged winter warfare.
Diplomatic efforts to find a peaceful resolution remain stalled, with both parties showing little willingness to compromise on core demands.

articles.headline: China's Economic Growth Faces Headwinds Amidst Global Slowdown
body: China's economic growth is reportedly facing significant headwinds, with recent data indicating a slowdown amidst a challenging global economic environment. Factors such as decreased export demand and ongoing property market issues are contributing to the moderated growth outlook.

The Chinese government has signaled its intention to implement further stimulus measures to support economic activity and stabilize key sectors. However, analysts suggest that structural reforms are also necessary to ensure sustainable long-term growth.
The global economic slowdown and geopolitical tensions are impacting China's trade relations and investment flows, prompting Beijing to focus on domestic consumption and technological self-reliance.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips and Rescinds AI Diffusion Rule
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (IFR) imposing new export controls on advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors and certain foreign data center activities involving remote access to computing power.

The rule formally rescinds the AI Diffusion Rule and introduces a new end-use-based license requirement for advanced computing items destined for non-U.S. data centers that provide remote access to a 'significant volume of compute power' to end users headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination (including China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, and Russia).

Additionally, the IFR establishes a new destination-based license requirement for exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of advanced computing items to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, due to the risk of diversion.
articles.source: Federal Register / U.S. Department of Commerce BIS

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
